## {data-menu-title="Learning Objectives"}

[Learning Objectives]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

- define a brain-computer interface and explain why it is needed;
- describe the stages of how a BCI works;
- distinguish invasive, partially invasive, and non-invasive BCIs;
- name common brain-signal recording methods and control paradigms;
- state the features, limitations, and ethical concerns of BCI;
- identify major application areas of BCI.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Think About It"}

[Think About It]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- A person with paralysis cannot move but can still **think about moving**. Could that thought move a machine?
- Is it acceptable for a company to **read or store your brain data**?
- Would you accept a brain implant to **improve memory or speed**, not just to treat illness?
- Can a computer really "read your mind"?
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Why BCI?"}

[Why Do We Need Brain-Computer Interfaces?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Millions of people live with **paralysis, spinal-cord injury, stroke, ALS, or loss of limbs**.
- Their brains may still **plan movement and speech**, but the path to muscles is broken.
- A BCI **bypasses the damaged pathway** and links the brain directly to a machine.
- It also opens new ways of **human-computer interaction** for everyone.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="What Is BCI?"}

[What Is a Brain-Computer Interface?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
A **Brain-Computer Interface (BCI)**, also called a brain-machine interface, is a system that creates a **direct communication pathway between the brain and an external device**, without relying on normal peripheral nerve and muscle output pathways.

- It **reads brain signals**, interprets them, and converts them into **commands** for a computer, wheelchair, prosthetic limb, or software.
- Some systems also **send signals back** to the brain, for example to restore sensation.
- The main goal is to **help people with disabilities** and extend human-computer interaction.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Brain Basics"}

[Brain Basics Behind BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- The brain contains about **86 billion neurons** that communicate with tiny **electrical signals**.
- Thinking, moving, or seeing makes groups of neurons **fire together**, producing recognisable electrical patterns.
- Different brain regions have different roles; for example, the **motor cortex** plans voluntary movement.
- A BCI **records these patterns** and learns which pattern corresponds to which intention.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="How BCI Works"}

[How Does a BCI Work?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Brain Activity] --> B[Signal Acquisition]
    B --> C[Signal Processing and Feature Extraction]
    C --> D[Decoding with Machine Learning]
    D --> E[Device Command]
    E --> F[External Device]
    F --> G[Feedback to the User]
    G --> A
```

::: {.body-text-s}
- **Acquire:** sensors record brain-related electrical, magnetic, or blood-oxygen signals, depending on the method.
- **Process:** noise and artefacts are reduced and useful features are extracted.
- **Decode:** trained models or other decoding algorithms map patterns to commands.
- **Act and feedback:** the device responds, and the user sees the result and adapts.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="BCI Components"}

[Main Components of a BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Component | Role | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Signal acquisition | Records brain signals using electrodes or sensors | EEG cap, implanted electrode array |
| Pre-processing | Amplifies and filters out noise and artefacts | Removing eye-blink and muscle noise |
| Feature extraction | Picks out useful patterns from the signal | Power in certain frequency bands |
| Classification / decoding | Translates features into commands | Machine-learning classifier |
| Output device | Carries out the command | Cursor, wheelchair, robotic arm, speller |
| Feedback | Shows the user the result so they can adjust | Screen display, vibration, sound |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Types of BCI"}

[Types of Brain-Computer Interfaces]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Type | Description | Example | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-invasive | Sensors on the scalp; no surgery | EEG headset | Lower procedural risk, but weaker and noisier signals |
| Partially invasive | Electrodes placed on the brain surface, inside the skull | ECoG (electrocorticography) | Better signals, needs surgery |
| Invasive | Electrodes implanted in the brain tissue | Microelectrode array implants | Detailed local signals; surgical and long-term implant risks |
:::

::: {.body-text-s}
By direction: **output BCIs** decode brain activity to control devices; **input interfaces** stimulate the brain to provide information (e.g., experimental cortical sensory feedback); **bidirectional BCIs** combine recording and stimulation. Terminology varies: ECoG is also commonly classified as invasive because it requires surgery.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Recording Methods"}

[Brain-Signal Recording Methods]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Method | What It Measures | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| EEG (electroencephalography) | Electrical activity from the scalp | Cheap, portable, most common non-invasive method |
| ECoG | Electrical activity from the brain surface | Higher quality than EEG; requires surgery |
| Intracortical electrodes | Spikes from neurons and/or local field potentials | Detailed local recordings; invasive |
| fNIRS | Blood oxygen changes using light | Non-invasive; slower response |
| MEG / fMRI | Magnetic fields / blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals | Used mainly in research; large and costly equipment |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Control Paradigms"}

[How Does the User Send Commands?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Motor imagery:** the user *imagines* moving a hand or foot, which creates a detectable pattern.
- **P300 speller:** the brain gives a characteristic response when the user sees the letter they want in a flashing grid.
- **SSVEP:** looking at a flickering light at a certain frequency produces a matching brain response.
- **Attention or relaxation level:** focus or calm states control simple devices or games.
- **Speech decoding:** newer research decodes the brain activity of attempted speech into text or voice.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="BCI Features"}

[Key Features of BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Direct brain-to-device communication:** no keyboard, mouse, or muscle movement needed.
- **Online operation:** some BCIs provide continuous control; latency ranges from fractions of a second to several seconds or longer, depending on sensing and task.
- **Adaptive:** both the user and the system learn and improve with practice.
- **Uses signals such as EEG:** electrical activity of the brain is recorded.
- **Supports feedback:** visual, auditory, or sensory feedback closes the loop.
- **Assistive and enhancing:** restores lost abilities and can support new ways of interaction.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Role of AI"}

[Role of AI and Machine Learning in BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Brain signals are **weak, noisy, and different for each person**, so decoding often needs user-specific calibration and careful validation.
- **Machine learning** learns each user's patterns during a **calibration session**.
- **Deep learning** can support movement and speech decoding when suitable training data are available; simpler methods can also be effective.
- Some systems **adapt** as signals change; others require periodic recalibration.
- Link to earlier topics: BCI generates a **stream of data** that is processed using signal processing, big data techniques, and AI.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Advantages"}

[Advantages of BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Restores independence** to people with severe disabilities.
- **Enables communication** for people who cannot speak or move.
- **Hands-free control** of devices and software.
- **Rehabilitation support:** helps retrain the brain after stroke.
- **Research value:** improves understanding of the brain.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="BCI Limitations"}

[Limitations and Challenges of BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Weak and noisy signals:** brain signals are small and mixed with other electrical activity.
- **Surgical risk:** invasive implants can cause infection and tissue damage.
- **Accuracy and speed:** much slower and less reliable than natural movement.
- **Training and calibration:** requirements vary by person, recording method, and control paradigm.
- **Cost and availability:** advanced implanted systems are largely investigational; simpler non-invasive systems have different capabilities.
- **Long-term stability:** implants may degrade or move over time.
- **Privacy and security:** brain data is highly personal and could be hacked or misused.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Ethics"}

[Ethical and Legal Concerns]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Mental privacy:** who owns and can use brain data?
- **Informed consent:** especially for patients who cannot easily communicate.
- **Safety and responsibility:** who is responsible if a BCI-controlled device causes harm?
- **Identity and autonomy:** does an implant change how a person acts or feels?
- **Fairness and access:** enhancement could widen the gap between those who can and cannot afford it.
- **Regulation:** clear laws and medical standards are still developing; the term **neurorights** is used for proposed protection of mental privacy.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="BCI Applications"}

[Application Areas of BCI]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Area | Use of BCI |
|---|---|
| Healthcare and rehabilitation | Supporting communication, device control, and rehabilitation; outcomes vary |
| Prosthetics | Thought-controlled artificial limbs |
| Communication | Letting patients with locked-in syndrome type or speak |
| Assistive devices | Controlling wheelchairs and smart-home devices |
| Gaming and entertainment | Hands-free control and immersive experiences |
| Neuroscience research | Studying brain activity and cognition |
| Education and training | Research into workload estimates; attention is not measured directly or reliably in every setting |
| Defence and safety | Monitoring pilot or driver alertness |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Related Technologies"}

[BCI and Other Unit V Technologies]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **AR/VR:** BCI can control virtual environments and help rehabilitation inside VR.
- **IoT and smart homes:** thought-based commands can switch devices on or off.
- **Big data and AI:** decode large volumes of brain-signal data.
- **Cloud:** stores and processes data for training decoders.
- **Green computing:** implants and wearables must be **energy efficient** and have long battery life.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Case Study"}

[Illustrative Research Scenario: Restoring Communication]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Problem:** a person with paralysis due to brain-stem stroke cannot speak or move.
- **BCI solution:** electrodes record activity from the brain region that controls speech or hand movement; a machine-learning decoder converts attempted speech or imagined handwriting into text on a screen.
- **Potential outcome:** communication without normal muscle output. Performance varies; BCI is not universally faster or more suitable than eye tracking, and it does not read arbitrary private thoughts.
- **Concerns:** surgery risk, device lifetime, cost, and protection of brain data.

**Lesson:** BCI can restore lost abilities, but safety, privacy, and ethics must be addressed together with technology.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Summary"}

[Lecture Summary]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- A BCI creates a direct link between the brain and an external device.
- It works by acquiring signals, processing them, decoding them with algorithms, often machine learning, controlling a device, and giving feedback.
- BCIs can be non-invasive (EEG), partially invasive (ECoG), or invasive (implanted electrodes).
- Applications include rehabilitation, prosthetics, communication, assistive devices, gaming, and research.
- Challenges include noisy signals, surgical risk, limited accuracy, cost, privacy, and ethics.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Knowledge Check"}

[Knowledge Check: MCQs]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
1. A BCI provides:  
   A. A direct link between the brain and a device  B. A faster hard disk  C. A new programming language  D. A type of printer  
   **Answer: A**

2. An EEG headset used as a BCI is an example of:  
   A. Invasive BCI  B. Non-invasive BCI  C. Cloud computing  D. Virtual reality only  
   **Answer: B**

3. Imagining a hand movement to control a cursor is called:  
   A. Motor imagery  B. Data mining  C. Virtualisation  D. Encryption  
   **Answer: A**

4. Which is a major concern with BCIs?  
   A. Mental privacy of brain data  B. They need no power  C. They never make errors  D. They cannot be used in medicine  
   **Answer: A**

5. The step that converts processed brain features into commands is:  
   A. Decoding or classification  B. Printing  C. Compiling  D. Paging  
   **Answer: A**
:::

## {data-menu-title="Key Concepts"}

[Important Definitions and Key Terminology]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
- **BCI:** a direct communication link between the brain and an external device.
- **Neuron:** a nerve cell that carries electrical signals.
- **EEG:** recording of the brain's electrical activity from the scalp.
- **ECoG:** recording from the surface of the brain, under the skull.
- **Motor imagery:** imagining a movement to generate a control signal.
- **P300 / SSVEP:** brain responses used to select letters or commands.
- **Decoding:** translating brain signals into commands using algorithms.
- **Neurofeedback:** showing users their brain activity so they can learn to control it.
- **Neurorights:** proposed rights protecting mental privacy and identity.
:::
